_deprecated.note: shipsTransiting, stranded, throughputPercent, transitsBaseline, insuranceMultiple, and status mix sources or are scalar projections of richer objects. status in particular switches producer (PortWatch, falling back to AIS) without saying which; use transits.*, insurance.*, dailyTransits.*, and verdict.status instead.

aisBaselineNote: transitsBaseline is withheld (null) until 72 hourly samples exist on the current tiled12-active30m-fix60 basis. The basis last reset on 2026-09-26, when vessels whose last AIS fix is an hour or more old stopped counting as holding position or moving; before that it reset on 2026-07-30 (tiling, counts up roughly 3.4x) and 2026-07-20 (30-minute window). After each reset the median is withheld for about 3 days while samples on the new basis build up. Samples on an earlier basis are not mixed in. It is an AIS concurrent-presence median, a different population from transits.baseline (IMF PortWatch daily crossings); do not divide one by the other.
aisFirstFixNote: aisConcurrentInZone counts only vessels whose movement was measured against an earlier position. aisFirstFixInZone counts vessels seen in the same window for the first time, which have nothing to compare against yet; they are in neither aisConcurrentInZone nor stranded.
aisGapCarryoverNote: aisGapCarryoverInZone counts vessels the feed listed again after we had not seen them for more than two hours. Their status dates from before that absence, so we have not seen them hold or move since. Single vessels drop off and return on most runs, so a count above zero does not mean our collection stopped. They are in none of aisConcurrentInZone, stranded, strandedOffshore or aisStaleFixInZone. A vessel on a first sighting can also be anchored, so the groups are a split by how status was observed, not terms that add up exactly.

aisGaps.countScope: count is a floor on hulls we stopped receiving, not a count of evasions. Read it against eligibleTankers, the screened tanker population, and against ambientDarkRate, the share of eligible non-tankers that went dark on the identical test. The tanker rate (36.0%) is running 1.3x the whole-box ambient rate (26.8%), but within the same waters, compared cell by cell, 64 tankers went dark against about 62 expected at the ambient rate there, so the excess is not distinguishable from ambient dropout.
aisGaps.vesselsTrackedScope: vesselsTracked is a cumulative, all-time, all-type total (every vessel ever recorded anywhere in the wider AIS bbox). It is not the screened population behind count: that population is tankers only, with 50 or more sightings, last seen inside the core area.

aisStaleFixNote: aisStaleFixInZone counts vessels still listed in the window whose last AIS fix was 60 minutes or more old when we read it. Their position is where they were, not where they are, so they are in none of aisConcurrentInZone, stranded or strandedOffshore. Of the stale vessels that reported again over three runs on 2026-09-26, 79 had not moved, 36 had moved and 15 had dropped off the feed, so the count left out is part held and part gone. Treat stranded and strandedOffshore as counts of vessels seen holding position within the last hour.

capeSnapshot.note: transitsLast24h counts port arrivals only (departures are not published upstream), across ports on both sides of the strait. Not a Hormuz crossing count. Use transits.count for that. An arrival is a port-area entry event rather than a distinct hull: adjacent ports double count and an anchorage reposition can re-trigger one, so read arrivals24hTotal as an activity index. expectedTotal is a 30-day forward book (ships expected within the next 30 days), not a queue waiting now. This feed is retired: the upstream port pages moved these aggregates behind a subscription on 2026-08-28 and have published none since, so the figures are frozen at asOf. For live Hormuz-corridor port activity use /api/v1/ports; for live Cape traffic use the cape row in chokepoints above.

carrierSuspensions.notes: Mediterranean Shipping Company routes Asia–Europe services via the Cape of Good Hope. Its March advisory suspended Middle East bookings and told ships in the area to shelter; it has published no vessel count since.

Maersk has suspended bookings to Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, Saudi Gulf ports, Jordan and most UAE ports. It discharges at Fujairah and Khor Fakkan, outside the strait, and moves cargo overland to Jebel Ali, and it charges USD 1,000 a container on any vessel that transits the Strait of Hormuz, on top of an Emergency Freight rate. Its Update 46 of 11 September 2026 sets that rate at USD 1,800 per 20-foot dry container, USD 3,000 per 40-foot dry container and USD 3,800 per reefer, special or dangerous-goods container, on cargo loading from or bound for Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia (Dammam and Jubail), Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE and Oman (except Salalah). The surcharge figure shown is the USD 1,000 per-container transit fee, not the Emergency Freight rate. It said on 25 June that three of its vessels remained in the Gulf.

CMA CGM has activated Cape of Good Hope routing for all Asia–Europe services. Its chief financial officer said on the second-quarter earnings call on 30 July that eight of its vessels were inside the Gulf and unable to exit through the strait.
carrierSuspensions.sourceName: CMA CGM Q2 earnings call, via WorldCargo News

carrierSuspensions.notes: COSCO Shipping has suspended bookings to Bandar Abbas and routes Europe-bound services via the Cape. Two of its container ships crossed the strait in late March with Iranian clearance; it has not published a Gulf posture or vessel count since.
Hapag-Lloyd has suspended Hormuz transits and reroutes via the Cape. By 1 July it had moved all four of its vessels out of the Gulf.
Ocean Network Express suspended new bookings to and from the Persian Gulf on 2 March 2026, citing safety for crew, vessels and cargo. No advisory newer than that has been found.

chokepointsNote: preCrisisBaselineMedian on every row is computed over one fixed window (baselineWindowStart to baselineWindowEnd) anchored to the Hormuz crisis. For hormuz that window is a genuine pre-crisis baseline. For bab-el-mandeb, suez and cape it is not: those routes were already carrying diverted Red Sea traffic within that window, so preCrisisBaselineMedian for those rows reads as wartime volume, not a peacetime figure. baselineMedian is a different figure: the median of the latest 30 daily counts (trailing 30 days), not the fixed window.

bullets: BREAKING: Iranian Major General Safavi says Tehran's main strategy is intelligent management of the Strait of Hormuz against the US naval blockade, per Defapress via Newsquawk; this has not been independently confirmed.
Two merchant vessels carrying 22 Indian crew were attacked in the strait, with two seafarers missing, per Telegraph India and ThePrint.
Brent stood at $105.95 as of 12:06 UTC, up 1.17% over 24 hours; IMF PortWatch recorded 4 transits on October 4, against a pre-crisis baseline of 85 per day.
dailyBrief.summary: The Strait of Hormuz remains under acute operational pressure, with commercial throughput recorded by IMF PortWatch at 4 transits on October 4, against a pre-crisis baseline of 85 per day. In the most significant development of this window, Iranian Major General Yahya Rahim Safavi has stated that Tehran's principal strategy is the intelligent management of the strait in response to the US naval blockade, per Defapress as relayed by Newsquawk; that claim has not been independently confirmed. Iranian state media separately carry a claim, via IRNA, that Iran intends to counter the US blockade through what it calls strategic management of the waterway, which must be treated as an unverified state-media assertion. On the attacks, two merchant vessels carrying 22 Indian crew were struck in the strait, with two seafarers reported missing, per Telegraph India and ThePrint. Around Prague separately headlines a second tanker hit by a projectile within 24 hours, while The Star, citing the UK Maritime Agency, reports a tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile with crew reported safe; those reports were carried in the prior window and no row in this feed names a different ship or position to distinguish them as new incidents. The IRGC claims an oil tanker struck a mine in the strait, per bernama and The Express Tribune; no maritime authority has confirmed that claim. A tanker was also reported struck off Qatar, 51 nautical miles from Madinat ash Shamal, with UKMTO logging 16 regional attacks, per Hellenic Shipping News. Brent stood at $105.95 as of 12:06 UTC, up 1.17% over 24 hours. As of 12:20 UTC, 131 AIS-visible vessels were holding position away from berth in the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf watch box, a count that leaves out ships within 25km of a working port. On the Hormuz Index, Crisis Pressure, the state composite, sits in the extreme band, flat over 24 hours, with its value set by physical transit deviation alone; the Escalation Forecast sits in the high band, flat over 24 hours, with the Brent-WTI forward spread as its top contributor.

dataHealthNote: dataHealth.events reflects producer health, not event recency, UNLESS no event has arrived for 12 hours, after which it falls back to the plain event-age gate, so a very quiet stretch beyond 12 hours can still read stale even with a healthy pipeline. Use dataHealth.events.verifiedAt for the newest event time.

narrative.summary: The Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed to commercial traffic since February 28, 2026. Iran re-declared it closed after the July ceasefire collapsed, and the war has spread to a second chokepoint, where control of the Yemeni side of the Bab el-Mandeb is contested: the Houthis took it in September, Yemen's Saudi-backed government said on October 5 that it had retaken the coast up to Mocha, the Houthis deny it, and Reuters couldn't verify the claim. US forces have destroyed Iranian tankers and Iran has fired missiles at US warships and bases, while merchant ships are being hit at more than one a day: a projectile hit the Kuwaiti supertanker Al Funtas in the strait on the evening of September 28, three more ships were hit on September 29, the Kuwaiti supertanker Kazimah III was set on fire on October 1, two more tankers were reported hit on October 2, on October 4 the product tanker Lipsi was hit in the engine room and left drifting, two more tankers were struck on the evening of October 4, a tanker was hit on October 5 and reported an engine-room fire, the LNG carrier Maran Gas Mystras was hit leaving the strait around October 4, on October 6 a projectile hit the Panama-flagged On Peace off Oman, injuring 12 of her crew, 11 of them Indian, per India's foreign ministry, and on the evening of October 7 UKMTO said a tanker about 51 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal, off Qatar, was hit by multiple projectiles with casualties; maritime security sources later named her as the chemical tanker Acers, with minor crew injuries, per Reuters. Reuters, citing three maritime security sources, reported on October 7 that at least 12 attacks hit tankers around the strait in the week of September 28 to October 5, the most in any week since the war began. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre hasn't said who fired. The Guard-linked Fars news agency said on October 3 that the Revolutionary Guard's navy had targeted seven "violating" tankers in five days, and Iranian state media say three Emirati tankers among those hit were on Iran's non-compliance list. On October 5 Guard forces warned a tanker north of Khasab, Oman, that it would be targeted unless it turned back, and it complied, per UKMTO. On September 23 a seafarer was killed when projectiles hit the bulk carrier Cape Dao off Oman. Drones launched from Iraq shut Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, the largest route around the strait, on September 11; it restarted at a low rate on September 22 and loadings at Yanbu resumed within the week, with Kpler putting flow near 2.65 million barrels a day on September 28, about half the pre-attack rate, per Reuters as carried by Baird Maritime; Saudi Aramco hasn't confirmed a figure. How much is moving is contested, and the answer depends on what is counted. Reuters, on provisional Kpler data, reported on October 5 that Middle East crude exports topped their pre-war average of about 18 million barrels a day on four days in late September. That total leans on routes around the strait and on ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman: DW, citing Kpler, says about 40% of the crude left the Gulf without crossing the strait in September. The National, citing Kpler, puts flows through the strait itself at 6.02 million barrels a day in September, less than a third of February's. Vessel counts, ours included, stay far below pre-war levels, though they can't see tankers that cross with AIS off. On the talks, foreign minister Abbas Araghchi set out a seven-day plan on September 25: the United States would release frozen assets, lift oil sanctions and end its blockade, fighting would stop, and Iran would reopen the strait on the seventh day. President Trump rejected it in public on September 26, and on September 30 Iran said it had received a US response, whose terms haven't been published. On October 4 parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the strait won't open until Iran's seven conditions, which he said rest on the June Islamabad Memorandum, are met; CNBC says they include an end to the US blockade and the release of Iranian assets. On October 1 the United States added sanctions on Iran's rail system and a shadow banking network. On October 6 President Trump said the strait "belongs to the United States of America" and that US forces sink Iranian ships that run the blockade with no oil aboard. Iran's oil minister, Mohsen Paknejad, resigned on October 4 with crude exports stalled under the blockade, and Hamid Bovard of the National Iranian Oil Company is acting minister, per Bloomberg. On October 7 Revolutionary Guard adviser Mohammad Reza Naqdi said, per the Guard-linked Fars agency, that the strait stays closed until Iran's demands are met and that routes Iran calls illegal will soon be blocked. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the strait is open and Iran has lost control of it, and US Central Command called the closure claim false. Vice President JD Vance told Reuters that Iran must make a meaningful cut to its enrichment capacity, and a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Washington must first meet Tehran's conditions before nuclear talks can start. On October 8 President Trump said the US won't attack Iran before the November 3 midterm elections and that the blockade stays in force, and Mohsen Rezaei, a former Revolutionary Guard commander, has since said that Washington's reply to Iran's proposal is "insufficient" and that Tehran isn't preparing a further answer, per Anadolu, citing Tasnim, so the talks have not moved. On October 9 Iranian media reported that tankers on routes Iran hasn't approved may have hit mines, which no maritime authority has confirmed and US Central Command disputes, saying it has cleared the primary lanes. The same day the Revolutionary Guard claimed a strike on an LPG tanker it named as the NV Sunshine, which no maritime authority has confirmed, and said ships using routes Iran hasn't approved will be pursued across the region, not only in the strait. Separately, UKMTO logged a projectile strike and fire on a vessel about 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera, UAE, without naming the ship or who fired. On October 10 and 11 UKMTO reported more outbound tankers hit on the port side by projectiles, with the crews reported safe, per gCaptain, and the Guard said supertankers had hit mines on both days, which no maritime authority has confirmed, per Mehr. On October 10 US Central Command said a US fighter jet disabled the propulsion of the Panama-flagged cargo ship Ocean Molica in the Gulf of Oman, with her crew unharmed, per Reuters. US Central Command says it had redirected 133 commercial vessels under the blockade by October 9, and Brent settled at $104.72 that day, per our own feed.

pipelineBypass.name: Petroline (East-West Pipeline)
pipelineBypass.notes: Saudi Aramco's East-West Pipeline carries Arabian Light from Abqaiq to Yanbu on the Red Sea, the single largest non-Hormuz route for Gulf crude. Saudi Arabia shut it as a precaution on 11 September 2026 after drones launched from Iraq struck it in the Riyadh and Medina areas, damaging pipeline equipment. Pumping restarted at a low rate on 22 September and tanker loadings at Yanbu resumed in the last week of September. Reuters reported on 29 September that two trade sources put Yanbu crude loadings at about 2 million barrels a day, and that Kpler estimated flow through the line at about 2.65 million barrels a day against roughly 5.5 million before the attack, with a full return possibly a month away. Bloomberg reported on 30 September that about half the flow had been restored, and Reuters, citing Kpler, reported on 5 October that Saudi Arabia was loading from both the Red Sea and the Gulf. Saudi Aramco has not confirmed the restart or a flow figure on the record, though Reuters reported that it sent customers an October loading schedule for Yanbu. The utilization shown is Kpler's 2.65 million against the 7 million nameplate, as of 28 September. Kpler expected flow to reach 3 to 4 million within days, but we have found no later published figure, so the row stays at the last one stated.
pipelineBypass.sourceName: EIA · World Oil Transit Chokepoints, Al Jazeera, CNN, Reuters via Baird Maritime (29 Sep 2026), Kpler (29 Sep 2026), Bloomberg via gCaptain (30 Sep 2026), Reuters via NBC News (5 Oct 2026)

premium.note: Machine-payable premium endpoints (x402, USDC on Base): full vessel manifest with sanctions cross-reference, hourly-bucket history (with gaps) capped at one year with actual depth growing daily, one-call snapshot, structured daily brief, single-vessel dossiers, bulk export, real-time streaming, threshold-alert webhooks, a Hormuz flag rollup, a shadow-fleet risk screen of the vessels active on AIS in the Persian Gulf window, bunker and marine-fuel prices, and a modeled war-risk premium nowcast. $0.01-$0.50 per request, no key or account. MCP connector at the mcp URL.

strandedNote: `stranded` counts vessels seen holding position within the last hour (from the half-hourly stranded rollup when it is current, as strandedOffshore is, else from the live positions), including ones at berth working cargo at regional ports such as Dubai and Abu Dhabi; a vessel with a stale AIS fix is left out and counted in aisStaleFixInZone instead, not folded into stranded. `strandedOffshore` excludes vessels within 25km of a working port and is the narrower figure the site's own narrative uses.

transits.cadenceNote: Completed daily transits (IMF PortWatch crossing count). Not the same as aisConcurrentInZone, which is a snapshot of vessels moving inside the wider Persian Gulf watch box right now, not the Strait channel itself.
transits.freshestDayNote: The newest PortWatch row is always a Sunday, because IMF publishes weekly on Tuesday against data carrying a ~2-day lag. Sunday is the lowest-traffic weekday in this series, so the freshest print reads low against the day before it even in a normal week. Compare it with earlier Sundays, or with baselineMedian, rather than with previousNTotal.

verdict.long: War-risk insurance has priced commercial transit through the Strait of Hormuz beyond the reach of most operators.
